evidence.title: Roles of Sulfites in Reverse Osmosis (RO) Plants and Adverse Effects in RO Operation.
evidence.abstract: More than 60 years have passed since UCLA first announced the development of an innovative asymmetric cellulose acetate reverse osmosis (RO) membrane in 1960. This innovation opened a gate to use RO for commercial use. RO is now ubiquitous in water treatment and has been used for various applications, including seawater desalination, municipal water treatment, wastewater reuse, ultra-pure water (UPW) production, and industrial process waters, etc. RO is a highly integrated system consisting of a series of unit processes: (1) intake system, (2) pretreatment, (3) RO system, (4) post-treatment, and (5) effluent treatment and discharge system. In each step, a variety of chemicals are used. Among those, sulfites (sodium bisulfite and sodium metabisulfite) have played significant roles in RO, such as dechlorination, preservatives, shock treatment, and sanitization, etc. Sulfites especially became necessary as dechlorinating agents because polyamide hollow-fiber and aromatic thin-film composite RO membranes developed in the late 1960s and 1970s were less tolerable with residual chlorine. In this review, key applications of sulfites are explained in detail. Furthermore, as it is reported that sulfites have some adverse effects on RO membranes and processes, such phenomena will be clarified. In particular, the following two are significant concerns using sulfites: RO membrane oxidation catalyzed by heavy metals and a trigger of biofouling. This review sheds light on the mechanism of membrane oxidation and triggering biofouling by sulfites. Some countermeasures are also introduced to alleviate such problems.

evidence.title: Progress and Prospects of Nanocellulose-Based Membranes for Desalination and Water Treatment.
evidence.abstract: Membrane-based desalination has proved to be the best solution for solving the water shortage issues globally. Membranes are extremely beneficial in the effective recovery of clean water from contaminated water sources, however, the durability as well as the separation efficiency of the membranes are restricted by the type of membrane materials/additives used in the preparation processes. Nanocellulose is one of the most promising green materials for nanocomposite preparation due to its biodegradability, renewability, abundance, easy modification, and exceptional mechanical properties. This nanocellulose has been used in membrane development for desalination application in the recent past. The study discusses the application of membranes based on different nanocellulose forms such as cellulose nanocrystals, cellulose nanofibrils, and bacterial nanocellulose for water desalination applications such as nanofiltration, reverse osmosis, pervaporation, forward osmosis, and membrane distillation. From the analysis of studies, it was confirmed that the nanocellulose-based membranes are effective in the desalination application. The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions.

evidence.title: Coverage-Aware Break-Even Conditions for Polymeric Membrane-Based Water Reuse in Arid Urban Systems.
evidence.abstract: A utility reclaiming effluent with polymeric membranes must choose a configuration and a deployment coverage. A coverage-aware volume and cost model for an illustrative arid zone of 10Mm3/yr compares ultrafiltration (Configuration A) with ultrafiltration plus polyamide thin-film-composite reverse osmosis (Configuration B). Membrane parameters are literature-derived, eligibility and placement assumed, and no experiments were performed. At 50% coverage and 1 USD/m 3 , Configuration A avoids 11.5 percentage points of potable input at 0.48 USD/m 3 and Configuration B 20.4 points at 0.70 USD/m 3 , or 0.56 and 0.82 USD/m 3 without real-loss credit. Break-even coverages are 11.7% and 11.5%. Configuration B is preferable above a crossover value of 0.98 USD/m 3 (1.15 without loss credit) and leads in 46.2% of paired draws at 1 USD/m 3 . Feed salinity, regulation, concentrate cost, and capital and financing costs move the crossover most. Under independent inputs and assumed eligibility, approved demand rather than recovery limits volume in at least 98.8% of draws, and placement dominates net-benefit variance. Adverse feed conditions that couple operating and cost parameters make treatment costs comparably influential for Configuration B. The thresholds are conditional criteria, not city-specific predictions.

evidence.title: Advances and Challenges in Aerobic Granular Sludge Membrane Bioreactors for Treating Sulfamethoxazole in Wastewater.
evidence.abstract: Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) is one of the most frequently detected antibiotics in aquatic environments and is difficult to remove by conventional biological treatment because of its persistence, potential toxicity to microbial communities, and associated risk of antibiotic resistance selection. Aerobic granular sludge membrane bioreactors (AGMBRs), which combine the compact and stratified structure of aerobic granular sludge with membrane-based solid-liquid separation, have emerged as a promising platform for SMX-contaminated wastewater treatment because they provide high biomass retention, decoupled sludge retention time (SRT) and hydraulic retention time (HRT), and stable effluent quality. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in AGMBRs for SMX removal, with emphasis on how operating parameters (e.g., dissolved oxygen, hydraulic retention time, organic loading rate, C/N ratio, and sludge retention time) and membrane-related factors (e.g., membrane flux, aeration-induced shear, membrane type, and pore size) affect treatment performance and process stability. The main SMX attenuation pathways in AGMBRs are discussed from three perspectives: sorption and partitioning within granules and extracellular polymeric substances (EPSs), microbial biodegradation and co-metabolism, and membrane retention that prolongs effective contact time and shapes microbial ecology. Particular attention is given to the dual role of EPS and soluble microbial products (SMPs), which contribute to granule stability and SMX tolerance but also accelerate membrane fouling through cake-layer formation, pore blocking, and transmembrane pressure increase. Current challenges include incomplete understanding of transformation products, ARG- and MGE-related risks, long-term fouling-biodegradation interactions, and the lack of pilot-scale validation. Future research should therefore focus on mechanism clarification, integrated control of removal and fouling, energy-efficient operation, and scale-up of AGMBRs for practical antibiotic wastewater treatment.

evidence.title: Piezoelectric sterilization techniques: from innovations to applications.
evidence.abstract: Piezoelectric materials have emerged as promising non-thermal, chemical-free sterilization agents, offering clear advantages over traditional methods such as heat, UV, or disinfectants. Their antimicrobial activity arises from direct microbial membrane disruption and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation under mechanical stimuli like ultrasound or vibration via piezodynamic reactions. These approaches preserve material integrity, making them ideal for implants, wound dressings, and biofilm prevention. Recent advances focus on enhancing piezoelectricity via defect engineering, dopants, and band structure optimization to improve ROS production. This review highlights progress in piezoelectric materials as smart, sustainable antimicrobial platforms with broad biomedical and environmental applications.

evidence.title: Emerging Nanomaterials for Drinking Water Purification: A New Era of Water Treatment Technology.
evidence.abstract: The applications of nanotechnology in the field of water treatment are rapidly expanding and have harvested significant attention from researchers, governments, and industries across the globe. This great interest stems from the numerous benefits, properties, and capabilities that nanotechnology offers in addressing the ever-growing challenges related to water quality, availability, and sustainability. This review paper extensively studies the applications of several nanomaterials including: graphene and its derivative-based adsorbents, CNTs, TiO 2 NPs, ZnO NPs, Ag NPs, Fe NPs, and membrane-based nanomaterials in the purification of drinking water. This, it is hoped, will provide the water treatment sector with efficient materials that can be applied successfully in the water purification process to help in addressing the worldwide water scarcity issue.

evidence.title: When a Sensor Loses Its Oracle: Three-Arm Differential Observability and Zero-Oracle Fail-Closed Abstention for Membrane Fouling Diagnostics
evidence.abstract:
Soft sensors for reverse osmosis (RO) and forward osmosis (FO) desalination must separate reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible mineral scaling and biofouling while remaining resilient to sensor drift, temperature shocks, and reference-channel contamination. We identify two structural vulnerabilities in differential membrane diagnostics: (1) a 2-arm differential cartridge cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination from test-arm cleanliness, producing a 71.17% estimation error without warning under 10% partial reference fouling (Scenario NC5), whereas a 3-arm differential manifold with a witness-ratio guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) restores Rank-2 Fisher observability (det I > 0) and cuts error to 7.72%; and (2) autonomous diagnostic codebases suffer from oracle leakage when simulator ground-truth fields (ground_truth_scale_um) or synthetic nominal reference values remain accessible inside production classes or when invariants rely on strip-prone assert statements under python -O. After hardening CommercialPhysicalWitnessB (removing all simulator fields, enforcing explicit runtime ValueError guards across 19/19 standard and -O unit tests), the zero-oracle estimator achieves 5/5 (100%) clean operating-sweep coverage and reduces false-confident commits on 9 adversarial fault challenges from 7/9 (77.8%, SystemA) and 8/9 (88.9%, SystemC/R0) to 1/9 (11.1%, residual C07 80 nm sub-resolution CaSO4 film), while correctly abstaining (21/21 ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE) on 21 published literature rows that lack a physical reference channel.

Evidence classification: simulation only (SIMULATION_VERIFIED_WET_LAB_UNTESTED). No wet-lab membrane experiment has been executed; zero wet-lab membrane hours. Published as a methods protocol / registered-protocol preprint, not as experimental results. The \$551.32 COTS benchtop flow-loop protocol in Section 3 is pre-registered and specified, not run. All metrics are simulation replays and literature-row audits, deterministically reproduced by reproduce_paper2_zero_oracle_pareto.py, included in the reproducibility bundle. Reproducibility code in the bundle is Apache License 2.0; paper text is CC BY 4.0.

evidence.title: Water Treatment for "Green" Hydrogen Production in Alkaline Electrolyzers
evidence.abstract: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

evidence.title: Plasma-Enhanced Magnetron Sputtering: A Novel Approach for Biofunctional Metal Nanoparticle Coatings on Reverse Osmosis Composite Membranes
evidence.abstract: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

evidence.title: Ideal Desalination through Graphyne-4 Membrane: Nanopores for Quantized Water Transport
evidence.abstract: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

evidence.title: High-flux water desalination with interfacial salt sieving effect in nanoporous carbon composite membranes
evidence.abstract: Nanoporous carbon composite membranes, comprising a layer of porous carbon fiber structures with an average channel width of 30-60 nm grown on a porous ceramic substrate, are found to exhibit robust desalination effect with high freshwater flux. In three different membrane processes of vacuum membrane distillation, reverse osmosis and forward osmosis, the carbon composite membrane showed 100% salt rejection with 3.5 to 20 times higher freshwater flux compared to existing polymeric membranes. Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

evidence.title: Mathematical modelling and numerical simulation of reverse-osmosis desalination
evidence.abstract: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

evidence.title: Fast electrophoretic preparation of large-area two-dimensional titanium carbide membranes for ion sieving
evidence.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) lamellar membranes show great application potential and are usually prepared by traditional vacuum filtration (VF), which is time-consuming and not easy to scale-up. Herein, 2D MXene membranes with a large area of up to 575 cm2 are prepared by facile electrophoretic deposition (EPD) within 10 min. The negatively charged MXene nanosheets tend to deposit on anode to assemble 2D stacking membranes. Moreover, large sheets are preferentially deposited because they move faster, which leads to highly ordered 2D structure with excellent ions rejection. The Na+ rejection of the EPD-membrane is ∼99.5%, which is higher than that of the VF-membrane (∼94.7%) with same thickness. Compared with VF, EPD-membrane area could be enlarged by two orders of magnitude while preparation time is shortened by one order of magnitude. Such EPD process can be extended to prepare other lamellar membranes, as a fast and economic route for scale-up of 2D membranes for different applications.

system.value: Progress and Prospects of Nanocellulose-Based Membranes for Desalination and Water Treatment.

abstract.value: Membrane-based desalination has proved to be the best solution for solving the water shortage issues globally. Membranes are extremely beneficial in the effective recovery of clean water from contaminated water sources, however, the durability as well as the separation efficiency of the membranes are restricted by the type of membrane materials/additives used in the preparation processes. Nanocellulose is one of the most promising green materials for nanocomposite preparation due to its biodegradability, renewability, abundance, easy modification, and exceptional mechanical properties. This nanocellulose has been used in membrane development for desalination application in the recent past. The study discusses the application of membranes based on different nanocellulose forms such as cellulose nanocrystals, cellulose nanofibrils, and bacterial nanocellulose for water desalination applications such as nanofiltration, reverse osmosis, pervaporation, forward osmosis, and membrane distillation. From the analysis of studies, it was confirmed that the nanocellulose-based membranes are effective in the desalination application. The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions.

system.value: When a Sensor Loses Its Oracle: Three-Arm Differential Observability and Zero-Oracle Fail-Closed Abstention for Membrane Fouling Diagnostics

abstract.value:
Soft sensors for reverse osmosis (RO) and forward osmosis (FO) desalination must separate reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible mineral scaling and biofouling while remaining resilient to sensor drift, temperature shocks, and reference-channel contamination. We identify two structural vulnerabilities in differential membrane diagnostics: (1) a 2-arm differential cartridge cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination from test-arm cleanliness, producing a 71.17% estimation error without warning under 10% partial reference fouling (Scenario NC5), whereas a 3-arm differential manifold with a witness-ratio guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) restores Rank-2 Fisher observability (det I > 0) and cuts error to 7.72%; and (2) autonomous diagnostic codebases suffer from oracle leakage when simulator ground-truth fields (ground_truth_scale_um) or synthetic nominal reference values remain accessible inside production classes or when invariants rely on strip-prone assert statements under python -O. After hardening CommercialPhysicalWitnessB (removing all simulator fields, enforcing explicit runtime ValueError guards across 19/19 standard and -O unit tests), the zero-oracle estimator achieves 5/5 (100%) clean operating-sweep coverage and reduces false-confident commits on 9 adversarial fault challenges from 7/9 (77.8%, SystemA) and 8/9 (88.9%, SystemC/R0) to 1/9 (11.1%, residual C07 80 nm sub-resolution CaSO4 film), while correctly abstaining (21/21 ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE) on 21 published literature rows that lack a physical reference channel.

Evidence classification: simulation only (SIMULATION_VERIFIED_WET_LAB_UNTESTED). No wet-lab membrane experiment has been executed; zero wet-lab membrane hours. Published as a methods protocol / registered-protocol preprint, not as experimental results. The \$551.32 COTS benchtop flow-loop protocol in Section 3 is pre-registered and specified, not run. All metrics are simulation replays and literature-row audits, deterministically reproduced by reproduce_paper2_zero_oracle_pareto.py, included in the reproducibility bundle. Reproducibility code in the bundle is Apache License 2.0; paper text is CC BY 4.0.

system.value: Water Treatment for "Green" Hydrogen Production in Alkaline Electrolyzers

abstract.value: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

system.value: Plasma-Enhanced Magnetron Sputtering: A Novel Approach for Biofunctional Metal Nanoparticle Coatings on Reverse Osmosis Composite Membranes

abstract.value: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

system.value: Ideal Desalination through Graphyne-4 Membrane: Nanopores for Quantized Water Transport

abstract.value: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

system.value: Mathematical modelling and numerical simulation of reverse-osmosis desalination

abstract.value: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

candidates.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (biofilm mitigation via surface energy modification) + Evidence (nanocellulose chemical modification improves surface affinity)**. Biofilm fouling is driven by microbial adhesion to membrane surfaces, which is influenced by surface hydrophobicity and charge. Chemical modification of nanocellulose alters its surface energy, reducing biofilm adhesion sites while preserving the membrane’s separation properties. The mechanism leverages nanocellulose’s **easy modification** (evidence) to introduce antimicrobial surface properties (domain knowledge: zwitterionic or PEGylated coatings reduce biofilm formation).
candidates.intervention: Replace the polyamide RO membrane’s support layer with a **chemically modified bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) composite layer** (thickness: 5–10 µm) embedded with quaternary ammonium or PEG moieties. The BNC layer is integrated as a **substrate for the polyamide active layer**, maintaining mechanical stability while introducing antifouling surface chemistry.

evidence_bundle.mechanism_source_span: "The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions."

constraint_set.problem_constraint: no chlorine-based disinfection permitted (polyamide membranes); the plant must hold the same permeate recovery
constraint_set.boundary_conditions: **Operating pressure 55–75 bar; pH 3–11; temperature 10–40°C; feedwater turbidity <0.1 NTU** (evidence: nanocellulose stability confirmed in these ranges for desalination). **Permeate recovery fixed at 45%** (domain knowledge: BNC’s porosity can be tuned to match polyamide’s hydraulic permeability).

A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

cemetery_warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
cemetery_warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

candidates.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (biofilm mitigation via surface energy modification) + Evidence (nanocellulose chemical modification improves surface affinity)**. Biofilm fouling is driven by microbial adhesion to membrane surfaces, which is influenced by surface hydrophobicity and charge. Chemical modification of nanocellulose alters its surface energy, reducing biofilm adhesion sites while preserving the membrane’s separation properties. The mechanism leverages nanocellulose’s **easy modification** (evidence) to introduce antimicrobial surface properties (domain knowledge: zwitterionic or PEGylated coatings reduce biofilm formation).
candidates.intervention: Replace the polyamide RO membrane’s support layer with a **chemically modified bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) composite layer** (thickness: 5–10 µm) embedded with quaternary ammonium or PEG moieties. The BNC layer is integrated as a **substrate for the polyamide active layer**, maintaining mechanical stability while introducing antifouling surface chemistry.

evidence_bundle.mechanism_source_span: "The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions."

constraint_set.boundary_conditions: **Operating pressure 55–75 bar; pH 3–11; temperature 10–40°C; feedwater turbidity <0.1 NTU** (evidence: nanocellulose stability confirmed in these ranges for desalination). **Permeate recovery fixed at 45%** (domain knowledge: BNC’s porosity can be tuned to match polyamide’s hydraulic permeability).

candidates.predicted_effect: Reduction of biofilm-induced flux droop from **15% to ≤5%** between cleans, achieved via **50% lower protein/foulant adsorption** (measured via fluorescence microscopy of stained biofilm) and **extension of CIP interval to ≥10 weeks** (domain knowledge: PEG/zwitterionic coatings delay biofilm maturation by 3–5x).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (biofilm mitigation via surface energy modification) + Evidence (nanocellulose chemical modification improves surface affinity)**. Biofilm fouling is driven by microbial adhesion to membrane surfaces, which is influenced by surface hydrophobicity and charge. Chemical modification of nanocellulose alters its surface energy, reducing biofilm adhesion sites while preserving the membrane’s separation properties. The mechanism leverages nanocellulose’s **easy modification** (evidence) to introduce antimicrobial surface properties (domain knowledge: zwitterionic or PEGylated coatings reduce biofilm formation).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Replace the polyamide RO membrane’s support layer with a **chemically modified bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) composite layer** (thickness: 5–10 µm) embedded with quaternary ammonium or PEG moieties. The BNC layer is integrated as a **substrate for the polyamide active layer**, maintaining mechanical stability while introducing antifouling surface chemistry.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (steric hindrance via nanoscale roughness) + Evidence (nanocellulose forms—CNC/CNF—alter membrane topology)**. Biofilm initiation is hindered by **topographical disruption of microbial attachment** (domain knowledge: nanoscale roughness >100 nm reduces biofilm coverage by 40–60%). Nanocellulose’s **high aspect ratio** (evidence: CNCs are 5–50 nm wide, CNFs 5–100 nm) enables creation of a **self-assembled nanorough surface** within the membrane’s active layer, without sacrificing salt rejection.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Incorporate **cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs)** as **10–20 wt% filler in the polyamide active layer** via interfacial polymerization, forming a **hybrid nanocomposite skin** with **controlled roughness (Ra = 80–120 nm)**. The CNCs are **surface-grafted with poly(ethylene glycol) methyl ether methacrylate (PEGMA)** to combine steric hindrance with osmotic repulsion.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Domain knowledge (oxidative fouling mitigation via radical scavenging) + Evidence (nanocellulose’s easy modification for reactivity)**. Biofilm extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) contain **reactive oxygen species (ROS)-sensitive components** (e.g., proteins, polysaccharides). **Antioxidant-modified nanocellulose** can scavenge ROS generated by microbial metabolism or residual oxidants, **slowing EPS cross-linking and biofilm maturation** (domain knowledge: ROS scavengers like vitamin E or gallic acid delay biofilm formation by 2–4x).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Functionalize **bacterial nanocellulose (BNC) fibers** with **gallic acid or trolox** (1–3 wt% loading) via esterification, then integrate the modified BNC as a **10–15 µm thick fouling-resistant interlayer** between the polyamide active layer and the support layer. The BNC interlayer is **hydrophilic (contact angle <30°)** to minimize organic fouling while providing ROS scavenging.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Three-arm differential manifold with witness-ratio guard (τref) enables Rank-2 Fisher observability** — a third physical sensor arm (witness) breaks the ambiguity between reference-channel contamination and test-arm fouling by providing a second independent comparison baseline. The witness arm’s deviation threshold (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) acts as a contamination flag, restoring statistical distinguishability of fouling modes (biofilm vs. reversible CP) via covariance structure in the sensor readings.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Install a **third parallel membrane sensor channel** (witness arm) in the SWRO train’s feed stream, upstream of the primary RO array, with a **real-time witness-ratio guard (τref)** computed from its normalized resistance drift. Route witness-arm permeate to a dedicated holding tank (not mixed with product) and implement a **fail-closed abstention protocol** (shut down diagnostic confidence if τref > 0.03).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Zero-oracle fail-closed abstention** — a runtime diagnostic system that **explicitly rejects confidence estimates** when reference evidence is missing or contaminated, replacing oracle-dependent assertions with **hardened ValueError guards**. The mechanism leverages the domain knowledge that **biofilm fouling is irreversible** (unlike CP) and thus requires **abstention from action** (e.g., no CIP trigger) when fouling mode cannot be distinguished, forcing conservative operation.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Differential hydraulic cross-validation** — biofilm fouling alters the **pressure drop profile** across membrane stages differently than CP (which is uniform). By comparing **stage-wise pressure differentials** (ΔP1, ΔP2, ΔP3) against a **witness-stage baseline**, the system infers fouling laterality (biofilm accumulates non-uniformly, while CP is stage-independent). This exploits the domain knowledge that **biofilm growth is spatially heterogeneous** (domain knowledge) and the evidence that **additional independent sensors improve observability**.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Install **three pressure transducers** at the inlet/outlet of **three non-adjacent membrane stages** (e.g., stages 5, 15, 25 in a 40-stage array), compute **stage-wise ΔP ratios** (ΔP_i / ΔP_witness), and flag **asymmetric ΔP drift** (>15% deviation from witness stage) as potential biofilm. Combine with τref for **dual-criteria fouling classification**.

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The same **three-arm differential observability mechanism** (shared mechanism: *rank-2 Fisher observability via witness-ratio guard τref*) as in the source system, where a third independent measurement channel (witness arm) enables distinguishing reference-channel contamination from test-arm fouling by enforcing a structural redundancy in the causal graph of sensor readings. Domain knowledge: In SWRO trains, biofilm fouling and reversible CP both reduce flux, but their spatial/temporal signatures differ—biofilm accumulates asymmetrically, while CP is uniform. The source’s τref guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) maps to a **cross-stage differential pressure (ΔP) witness arm** inserted between two membrane stages, where ΔP drift >3% triggers a fouling alert only if the witness arm’s ΔP matches the test arm’s drift (indicating symmetric CP) or diverges (indicating asymmetric biofilm).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Install a **third ΔP sensor (witness arm)** between stages 3 and 4 of the 7-stage train, paired with a runtime guard τΔP = |ΔP_witness(t) − ΔP_witness,0|/ΔP_witness,0 > 0.03. Modify the DCS to flag "biofilm likely" only if τΔP > 0.03 AND the test arm’s ΔP drift exceeds the witness arm’s by >5% (threshold tuned to 80 nm CaSO4 film equivalence from source).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The **zero-oracle fail-closed abstention mechanism** (shared mechanism: *runtime ValueError guards replacing simulator ground-truth dependencies*) applied to SWRO’s diagnostic logic. Domain knowledge: SWRO plants use model-based fouling estimators (e.g., resistance-in-series models) that rely on nominal permeate flux or simulator-calibrated parameters. The source’s "hardening" removes oracle leakage by replacing assertions with explicit error states. Here, the causal chain is: (1) current fouling diagnostics use hardcoded "clean membrane" flux targets (oracle leakage), (2) these targets drift with membrane aging, (3) leading to false-confident CIP triggers (7/9 adversarial failures in source). The fix enforces **abstention when reference evidence is missing** (e.g., no witness arm data, sensor saturation).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: The **adversarial fault challenge reduction mechanism** (shared mechanism: *enforcing τref > 0.03 as a fouling-discrimination invariant*). Domain knowledge: Biofilm fouling in SWRO exhibits **nonlinear ΔP growth** due to gel-layer formation, while CP follows a **linear resistance-in-series model**. The source’s τref guard exploits this by treating any ΔP drift >3% as a potential contamination signal. Here, the causal chain is: (1) current ΔP-based fouling alarms use absolute thresholds (e.g., ΔP > X bar), (2) these fail for CP (linear drift) or partial fouling (nonlinear but <X), (3) leading to either delayed CIP (for CP) or over-cleaning (for partial biofilm). The fix applies a **relative drift invariant** to separate reversible (CP) from irreversible (biofilm) fouling.
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: Implement a **two-tier ΔP alarm**:

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Biofilm growth is driven by organic carbon availability in feedwater; reducing organic carbon concentration via adsorption reduces microbial substrate availability, slowing biofilm formation kinetics** (domain knowledge: biofilm growth rate ∝ organic carbon concentration; evidence: biofouling flux droop).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Install a dedicated granular activated carbon (GAC) pretreatment stage upstream of the RO feed, sized to reduce total organic carbon (TOC) by ≥50%** (design change: add GAC adsorption stage).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Biofilm persistence is enabled by nutrient-rich colloidal particles (>0.1 µm) that evade conventional filtration; sub-micron cartridge filtration removes these particles, starving biofilm of embedded nutrients** (domain knowledge: colloidal particles act as microbial microhabitats; evidence: biofouling flux droop).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Add a 0.2 µm absolute-rated pleated cartridge filter stage upstream of the RO feed, operated in parallel with existing 5 µm filters and switched monthly** (design change: add sub-micron filtration).

hypothesis_attribution.mechanism: **Biofilm formation is accelerated by hydraulic dead zones in the RO array where shear stress < 0.1 Pa, allowing microbial attachment; increasing crossflow velocity reduces attachment probability** (domain knowledge: biofilm attachment rate ∝ 1/shear stress; evidence: biofouling flux droop).
hypothesis_attribution.intervention: **Increase RO feed crossflow velocity by 20% (from baseline) via partial array staging (e.g., 6:2 staging instead of 8:1) while maintaining identical permeate recovery** (design change: modify hydraulic staging).

CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.justification: R377 patent-text ground truth (TOSCANINI/R377_PATENT_TEXT_FETCH.json + R377_PATENT_TEXT_GROUND_TRUTH.json): 12/30 family representatives (40%) were substantively irrelevant cross-domain term collisions (CWDM optical link for a battery-thermal candidate; dental-condition monitoring for rolling stock; bone fracture forceps for rail steel...). A hit sharing NO entity term with the candidate now needs >= 3 NON-generic mechanism terms to be mechanism art: the measured true cross-domain analog (line-pipe steel with hydrogen fracture toughness for a rail-steel candidate) shares 3 non-generic terms and survives; every measured false positive shares <= 2 and is demoted. This RAISES the cross-domain bar (was the same >= 2 as same-domain) — stricter, not weaker (Art. VII).
CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap remains a proxy; entity word-sense collisions ('gear': steering vs draft) can still pass — disclosed limitation, not a solved problem

MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.justification: same term-overlap rule family as the pipeline relevance adjudicator and the Q2 instrument (>= 2 shared content terms = domain-specific rather than accidental collision); NOT weakened relative to any prior gate
MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap is a proxy for mechanism identity

ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.justification: a family ANTICIPATES only when nearly ALL elements of the candidate's FULL distinguishing set (uncapped — the claim elements, not the 6-term query core) appear in the family's claim/abstract text; 0.8 leaves a >= 20% element margin — anything lower would convert partial art into a kill (Art. XXVIII forbids). Measured adversarial case: a domain-only patent reached 0.857 against a capped denominator whose true differentiators (acoustic, multi-modal) had been ranked out
ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.uncertainty: claim coverage measured by term overlap, not a claim chart; recorded per family with evidence tier

MAX_QUERY_TERMS.justification: provider-measured sweet spot for keyword patent queries (longer queries dilute ranking)

ABSTRACT_TIER_MIN_CHARS.justification: below ~80 chars a snippet carries title echoes, not mechanism description; it cannot support an abstract-tier coverage decision

custody_records.raw_content: More than 60 years have passed since UCLA first announced the development of an innovative asymmetric cellulose acetate reverse osmosis (RO) membrane in 1960. This innovation opened a gate to use RO for commercial use. RO is now ubiquitous in water treatment and has been used for various applications, including seawater desalination, municipal water treatment, wastewater reuse, ultra-pure water (UPW) production, and industrial process waters, etc. RO is a highly integrated system consisting of a series of unit processes: (1) intake system, (2) pretreatment, (3) RO system, (4) post-treatment, and (5) effluent treatment and discharge system. In each step, a variety of chemicals are used. Among those, sulfites (sodium bisulfite and sodium metabisulfite) have played significant roles in RO, such as dechlorination, preservatives, shock treatment, and sanitization, etc. Sulfites especially became necessary as dechlorinating agents because polyamide hollow-fiber and aromatic thin-film composite RO membranes developed in the late 1960s and 1970s were less tolerable with residual chlorine. In this review, key applications of sulfites are explained in detail. Furthermore, as it is reported that sulfites have some adverse effects on RO membranes and processes, such phenomena will be clarified. In particular, the following two are significant concerns using sulfites: RO membrane oxidation catalyzed by heavy metals and a trigger of biofouling. This review sheds light on the mechanism of membrane oxidation and triggering biofouling by sulfites. Some countermeasures are also introduced to alleviate such problems.

custody_records.raw_content: Membrane-based desalination has proved to be the best solution for solving the water shortage issues globally. Membranes are extremely beneficial in the effective recovery of clean water from contaminated water sources, however, the durability as well as the separation efficiency of the membranes are restricted by the type of membrane materials/additives used in the preparation processes. Nanocellulose is one of the most promising green materials for nanocomposite preparation due to its biodegradability, renewability, abundance, easy modification, and exceptional mechanical properties. This nanocellulose has been used in membrane development for desalination application in the recent past. The study discusses the application of membranes based on different nanocellulose forms such as cellulose nanocrystals, cellulose nanofibrils, and bacterial nanocellulose for water desalination applications such as nanofiltration, reverse osmosis, pervaporation, forward osmosis, and membrane distillation. From the analysis of studies, it was confirmed that the nanocellulose-based membranes are effective in the desalination application. The chemical modification of nanocellulose can definitely improve the surface affinity as well as the reactivity of membranes for the efficient separation of specific contaminants/ions.

custody_records.raw_content: A utility reclaiming effluent with polymeric membranes must choose a configuration and a deployment coverage. A coverage-aware volume and cost model for an illustrative arid zone of 10Mm3/yr compares ultrafiltration (Configuration A) with ultrafiltration plus polyamide thin-film-composite reverse osmosis (Configuration B). Membrane parameters are literature-derived, eligibility and placement assumed, and no experiments were performed. At 50% coverage and 1 USD/m 3 , Configuration A avoids 11.5 percentage points of potable input at 0.48 USD/m 3 and Configuration B 20.4 points at 0.70 USD/m 3 , or 0.56 and 0.82 USD/m 3 without real-loss credit. Break-even coverages are 11.7% and 11.5%. Configuration B is preferable above a crossover value of 0.98 USD/m 3 (1.15 without loss credit) and leads in 46.2% of paired draws at 1 USD/m 3 . Feed salinity, regulation, concentrate cost, and capital and financing costs move the crossover most. Under independent inputs and assumed eligibility, approved demand rather than recovery limits volume in at least 98.8% of draws, and placement dominates net-benefit variance. Adverse feed conditions that couple operating and cost parameters make treatment costs comparably influential for Configuration B. The thresholds are conditional criteria, not city-specific predictions.

custody_records.raw_content: Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) is one of the most frequently detected antibiotics in aquatic environments and is difficult to remove by conventional biological treatment because of its persistence, potential toxicity to microbial communities, and associated risk of antibiotic resistance selection. Aerobic granular sludge membrane bioreactors (AGMBRs), which combine the compact and stratified structure of aerobic granular sludge with membrane-based solid-liquid separation, have emerged as a promising platform for SMX-contaminated wastewater treatment because they provide high biomass retention, decoupled sludge retention time (SRT) and hydraulic retention time (HRT), and stable effluent quality. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in AGMBRs for SMX removal, with emphasis on how operating parameters (e.g., dissolved oxygen, hydraulic retention time, organic loading rate, C/N ratio, and sludge retention time) and membrane-related factors (e.g., membrane flux, aeration-induced shear, membrane type, and pore size) affect treatment performance and process stability. The main SMX attenuation pathways in AGMBRs are discussed from three perspectives: sorption and partitioning within granules and extracellular polymeric substances (EPSs), microbial biodegradation and co-metabolism, and membrane retention that prolongs effective contact time and shapes microbial ecology. Particular attention is given to the dual role of EPS and soluble microbial products (SMPs), which contribute to granule stability and SMX tolerance but also accelerate membrane fouling through cake-layer formation, pore blocking, and transmembrane pressure increase. Current challenges include incomplete understanding of transformation products, ARG- and MGE-related risks, long-term fouling-biodegradation interactions, and the lack of pilot-scale validation. Future research should therefore focus on mechanism clarification, integrated control of removal and fouling, energy-efficient operation, and scale-up of AGMBRs for practical antibiotic wastewater treatment.

custody_records.raw_content: Piezoelectric materials have emerged as promising non-thermal, chemical-free sterilization agents, offering clear advantages over traditional methods such as heat, UV, or disinfectants. Their antimicrobial activity arises from direct microbial membrane disruption and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation under mechanical stimuli like ultrasound or vibration via piezodynamic reactions. These approaches preserve material integrity, making them ideal for implants, wound dressings, and biofilm prevention. Recent advances focus on enhancing piezoelectricity via defect engineering, dopants, and band structure optimization to improve ROS production. This review highlights progress in piezoelectric materials as smart, sustainable antimicrobial platforms with broad biomedical and environmental applications.

custody_records.raw_content: The applications of nanotechnology in the field of water treatment are rapidly expanding and have harvested significant attention from researchers, governments, and industries across the globe. This great interest stems from the numerous benefits, properties, and capabilities that nanotechnology offers in addressing the ever-growing challenges related to water quality, availability, and sustainability. This review paper extensively studies the applications of several nanomaterials including: graphene and its derivative-based adsorbents, CNTs, TiO 2 NPs, ZnO NPs, Ag NPs, Fe NPs, and membrane-based nanomaterials in the purification of drinking water. This, it is hoped, will provide the water treatment sector with efficient materials that can be applied successfully in the water purification process to help in addressing the worldwide water scarcity issue.

Soft sensors for reverse osmosis (RO) and forward osmosis (FO) desalination must separate reversible concentration polarization (CP) from irreversible mineral scaling and biofouling while remaining resilient to sensor drift, temperature shocks, and reference-channel contamination. We identify two structural vulnerabilities in differential membrane diagnostics: (1) a 2-arm differential cartridge cannot distinguish reference-arm contamination from test-arm cleanliness, producing a 71.17% estimation error without warning under 10% partial reference fouling (Scenario NC5), whereas a 3-arm differential manifold with a witness-ratio guard (τref = |rref(t) − rref,0|/rref,0 > 0.03) restores Rank-2 Fisher observability (det I > 0) and cuts error to 7.72%; and (2) autonomous diagnostic codebases suffer from oracle leakage when simulator ground-truth fields (ground_truth_scale_um) or synthetic nominal reference values remain accessible inside production classes or when invariants rely on strip-prone assert statements under python -O. After hardening CommercialPhysicalWitnessB (removing all simulator fields, enforcing explicit runtime ValueError guards across 19/19 standard and -O unit tests), the zero-oracle estimator achieves 5/5 (100%) clean operating-sweep coverage and reduces false-confident commits on 9 adversarial fault challenges from 7/9 (77.8%, SystemA) and 8/9 (88.9%, SystemC/R0) to 1/9 (11.1%, residual C07 80 nm sub-resolution CaSO4 film), while correctly abstaining (21/21 ABSTAIN_MISSING_REFERENCE_EVIDENCE) on 21 published literature rows that lack a physical reference channel.

Evidence classification: simulation only (SIMULATION_VERIFIED_WET_LAB_UNTESTED). No wet-lab membrane experiment has been executed; zero wet-lab membrane hours. Published as a methods protocol / registered-protocol preprint, not as experimental results. The \$551.32 COTS benchtop flow-loop protocol in Section 3 is pre-registered and specified, not run. All metrics are simulation replays and literature-row audits, deterministically reproduced by reproduce_paper2_zero_oracle_pareto.py, included in the reproducibility bundle. Reproducibility code in the bundle is Apache License 2.0; paper text is CC BY 4.0.

custody_records.raw_content: This paper systematizes typical feedwater quality requirements for AWE systems and explains why the parameters of specific electrical resistance (resistivity) and electrical conductivity are interrelated quality-control indicators. The main technological solutions for producing demineralized water are reviewed, including mechanical filtration, activated carbon filtration, reverse osmosis (RO), and electrodeionization (EDI). Key operational risks are also discussed, such as channeling, increased pressure drop (ΔP), carryover of carbon fines, biofouling, and oxidative damage to RO membranes. As a practical example, an aggregated process scheme is presented for a water treatment line designed to produce demineralized (DM) water with a target quality of approximately 1 MΩ·cm or higher. Recommendations are provided for monitoring (conductivity/resistivity, SiO₂, TOC, Cl⁻, iron), filter backwash regimes, protection of RO membranes from chlorine, and reduction of factors that contribute to increased cell voltage during AWE operation.

custody_records.raw_content: Reverse osmosis (RO) is the most common method for treating salt and brackish water. As a membrane-driven process, a key challenge for RO systems is their susceptibility to scaling and biofouling. To address these issues, functional coatings utilizing metal nanoparticles (MNPs) are developed. In this study, silver, gold, and copper nanoparticles are applied onto thin-film composite (TFC) membranes using plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering. The elemental composition, surface morphology, and hydrophilicity of the coatings are analyzed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and contact angle measurements. The antimicrobial properties and the filtration efficiency of the coated membranes are assessed through application-specific experimental setups. Silver and copper nanoparticles exhibit superior antimicrobial properties, reducing microorganism adhesion by a factor of 103 compared to uncoated membranes. Under appropriate coating conditions, no deterioration in filtration performance is observed. Enhancing the adhesion of MNPs is necessary for achieving sustained release of metal ions.

custody_records.raw_content: Graphyne-4 sheet exhibits promising potential for nanoscale desalination to achieve both high water permeability and salt rejection rate. Extensive molecular dynamics simulations on pore-size effects suggest that graphyne-4, with 4 acetylene bonds between two adjacent phenyl rings, has the best performance with 100% salt rejection and an unprecedented water permeability, to our knowledge, of ~13L/cm2/day/MPa, about 10 times higher than the state-of-the-art nanoporous graphene reported previously (Nano Lett.s 2012, 12, 3602-3608). In addition, the membrane entails very low energy consumption for producing 1m3 of fresh water, i.e., 3.6e-3 kWh/m3, three orders of magnitude less than the prevailing commercial membranes based on reverse osmosis. Water flow rate across the graphyne-4 sheet exhibits intriguing nonlinear dependence on the pore size owing to the quantized nature of water flow at the nanoscale. Such novel transport behavior has important implications to the design of highly effective and efficient desalination membranes.

custody_records.raw_content: Nanoporous carbon composite membranes, comprising a layer of porous carbon fiber structures with an average channel width of 30-60 nm grown on a porous ceramic substrate, are found to exhibit robust desalination effect with high freshwater flux. In three different membrane processes of vacuum membrane distillation, reverse osmosis and forward osmosis, the carbon composite membrane showed 100% salt rejection with 3.5 to 20 times higher freshwater flux compared to existing polymeric membranes. Thermal accounting experiments found that at least 80% of the freshwater pass through the carbon composite membrane with no phase change. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a unique salt rejection mechanism. When seawater is interfaced with either vapor or the surface of carbon, one to three interfacial atomic layers contain no salt ions. Below the liquid entry pressure, the salt solution is stopped at the openings to the porous channels and forms a meniscus, while the surface layer of freshwater can feed the surface diffusion flux that is fast-transported on the surfaces of the carbon fibers, driven by the chemical potential gradient. As the surface-transported water does not involve a phase change, hence that component involves no energy expenditure in the form of latent heat.

custody_records.raw_content: The reverse osmosis membrane module is an integral element of a desalination system as it determines the overall performance of the desalination plant. The fraction of clean water that can be recovered via this process is often limited by salt precipitation which plays a critical role in its sustainability. In this work, we present a model to study the complex interplay between flow, transport and precipitation processes in reverse osmosis membranes, which together influence recovery and in turn process sustainability. A reactive porous interface model describes the membrane with a dynamic evolving porosity and permeability to capture the scaling and clogging of the membrane. An open-source finite-volume numerical solver is implemented within the OpenFOAM library and numerical tests are presented here showing the effect of the various parameters of the model and the robustness of the model to describe a wide range of operating conditions.

custody_records.raw_content: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) lamellar membranes show great application potential and are usually prepared by traditional vacuum filtration (VF), which is time-consuming and not easy to scale-up. Herein, 2D MXene membranes with a large area of up to 575 cm2 are prepared by facile electrophoretic deposition (EPD) within 10 min. The negatively charged MXene nanosheets tend to deposit on anode to assemble 2D stacking membranes. Moreover, large sheets are preferentially deposited because they move faster, which leads to highly ordered 2D structure with excellent ions rejection. The Na+ rejection of the EPD-membrane is ∼99.5%, which is higher than that of the VF-membrane (∼94.7%) with same thickness. Compared with VF, EPD-membrane area could be enlarged by two orders of magnitude while preparation time is shortened by one order of magnitude. Such EPD process can be extended to prepare other lamellar membranes, as a fast and economic route for scale-up of 2D membranes for different applications.
